items.prompt: Per this unit, what is "power" in an organizational sense?
choices: Being liked by leadership
The ability to actually get a decision adopted, funded, staffed, and sustained — a real, distinct resource separate from being technically correct
Having the most senior title in the room
Being the loudest or most persistent voice in a meeting
items.explanation: Power is specifically the capability to make things happen — allocate resources, get something prioritized, get a team to change direction. It's explicitly distinguished from being liked, being senior, or being loud, none of which guarantee that capability.

items.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the four sources of power described in L2?
choices: Formal authority (control over budget/headcount/roadmap)
Expertise (a track record that makes your judgment trusted)
Seniority by tenure alone, independent of the other three
Information (context about what decision-makers actually care about)
items.explanation: The four sources named are formal authority, expertise, relationships, and information. Tenure alone isn't listed as a source — someone can accumulate any of the four sources without long tenure, and long tenure with none of the four doesn't by itself confer power in this framework.

items.prompt: In L2's model, why is technical correctness described as "necessary but not sufficient" for a proposal's adoption?
choices: Because correctness is actually irrelevant to whether a proposal is adopted
Because correctness gets a proposal to the point of being considered, but adoption also requires reaching someone with the power to act on it and finding it worth their while
Because only formally-authorized proposals can ever be considered
Because incorrect proposals are adopted just as often as correct ones
items.explanation: A correct proposal that never reaches anyone with the power to act, or reaches them but isn't framed around anything they're accountable for, gets shelved — not because it's wrong, but because correctness alone doesn't move the adoption pipeline forward.

items.prompt: In L3, what was the key difference between Attempt 2 (shelved) and Attempt 3 (adopted), given the underlying proposal was technically identical in both?
choices: Attempt 3 involved a completely different, less risky technical design
Attempt 3 reached a different, more senior sponsor than Attempt 2
Attempt 3 framed the same proposal around a metric (on-call sustainability) the sponsor was personally accountable for, rather than around the proposal's own correctness
Attempt 3 succeeded purely by chance, with no identifiable cause
items.explanation: Both attempts reached the same sponsor with the same technical proposal. Attempt 2 argued the idea was correct and important; Attempt 3 connected the same proposal to a metric the sponsor was already being measured on — the framing, not the substance or the sponsor, is what changed.

items.prompt: Per L3's failure modes, what's the distinction between the incentive-aligned framing used in Attempt 3 and a dishonest manipulation of the sponsor?
choices: There is no distinction — both are equally manipulative

The Attempt 3 framing emphasized a real, true effect of the proposal (reduced on-call bottleneck) that simply hadn't been foregrounded before — dishonest framing would mean fabricating a connection that isn't actually true
Framing is only honest if it's presented in writing rather than in conversation
Framing is only honest if the sponsor is told explicitly that persuasion is being attempted
items.explanation: L3 explicitly warns against fabricating a connection to a sponsor's incentives — the on-call framing worked because it was already a true property of the proposal, just not yet the one being emphasized. A sponsor discovering a framing was hollow spends trust that's expensive to rebuild.

items.prompt: Per L3's last failure mode, does the correctness-sponsor-framing pipeline only apply to large, visible proposals like the rollback automation case?
choices: Yes — smaller requests like a code review pushback don't involve power dynamics at all
No — the same three-part pattern applies at any scale, including small process changes or a single code review disagreement; the large scenario is just used to make each part easier to see
No, but it only applies to requests that involve money
Yes, the pattern is specific to infrastructure and reliability proposals
items.explanation: L3 states directly that the same pipeline (technical merit, reaching someone with relevant power, framing matched to their incentives) governs decisions at every scale — the scenario was chosen to be large mainly so each part of the pipeline is legible, not because the pattern is scale-specific.
